caveat: The author is a central figure in the field being assessed, so read it as a position paper. Metadata only; abstract not read.
title: The state of degrowth research and how to assess it
why: A stock-take of degrowth scholarship by one of its architects. Low keyword fit, but it sits directly behind the degrowth-curriculum and epistemic-justice material already on the radar.
abstract: Abstract This article addresses two inter-related questions. First, are degrowth claims supported by empirical evidence? And second, how do we go about reviewing the literature to answer this question? We analyze five recent reviews on the state of degrowth research focusing on the more critical, outlier of the five studies, and compare it with the four others in terms of their findings and in terms of their approach to reviewing the literature. In terms of evidence, our main finding is that the core claim of degrowth research, that green growth is unlikely if not impossible, is well supported by now; tentative findings also support the feasibility of degrowth-oriented pathways. In terms of review practice, we find that a good review of an interdisciplinary sustainability field like degrowth should avoid disciplinary biases, be transparent about its own assumptions, and use methods that are fit for the purposes it sets for itself.
